Modernization · Proof of concept

Migrating Oracle Forms to Vaadin with AI: what actually generalizes

Vaadin 25 + Spring Boot 4 Oracle Summit · ORDERS form Draft

The question: can an Oracle Forms master-detail block — an order with its line items, trigger-driven totals, an LOV-backed product lookup, optimistic locking — become a Vaadin Grid-and-form? And, more usefully: where does it break, and which of those breaks can a tool learn so it never breaks again?

This is the write-up of a time-boxed proof of concept. We took one representative slice of the Oracle Summit demo schema — the ORDERS form, S_ORD master / S_ITEM detail — and migrated it to Vaadin 25 + Spring Boot 4, with the migration itself driven by a set of composable AI skills. The app runs against a real Oracle database in a Docker container, and every migrated construct ships with a browser test that drives it end-to-end.

The migration is the vehicle. The finding is the payoff.

The finding: AI-assisted modernization is a sorting problem

Here is the thesis the whole POC exists to argue. Every correction you make to AI-generated code is one of exactly two things:

  • Generalizable — a rule the tool should have known. You push it back into the mapping ruleset, and it now works for every form, forever.
  • Specific — an irreducible quirk of this form. You hand-fix it, log it, and move on. It teaches the tool nothing.

The reusable asset is the accumulated generalizable set. It gets smarter every time a fix is sorted correctly.

The single number a Forms-shop architect actually cares about is the ratio of generalizable-to-specific fixes — because that ratio is their automation ceiling.

One rule keeps this honest: a fix is "specific" by default. It only earns "generalizable" status when the rule behind it can be stated in form-construct terms — "any table-level audit trigger stays in the database", not "the ORDERS header needed an extra field". If you can't articulate the rule generically, you log it as specific. That conservatism is exactly what separates a reusable skill from one quietly overfit to Summit.

Why this is hard (and why a naive port misses it)

An Oracle Forms .fmb is not a UI layout. It is a dense bundle of:

  • blocks bound to base tables, with master-detail relations that keep a header and its lines navigating together;
  • triggers (the ORDERS form has 45 of them) carrying validation, defaulting, query and commit logic in PL/SQL;
  • items whose type carries meaning — a Radio Group says "small fixed choice", an LOV says "lookup", a Display Item says "computed, read-only";
  • frames and boilerplate text that group fields and title sections;
  • LOVs and record groups backing type-ahead lookups;
  • a locking and commit model (COMMIT_FORM) that flushes the whole master-detail graph as one unit.

A migration that only looks at the screen drops most of this silently. The interesting work is deciding, construct by construct, what each of these becomes on the web — and being honest about what doesn't survive the trip.

The architecture we landed on

We routed every datum through a strict, testable layering:

View ← Presenter ← Service ← Domain ← (JdbcClient) ← Data
  • Domain owns the formula — pure, unit-testable computation. The order total is Order.total(), a Sum over each line's itemTotal(); the per-order next line id is Order.nextItemId() (the Forms PRE-INSERT rule NVL(MAX(item_id),0)+1). This is where declarative Forms calculations and WHEN-VALIDATE-* logic land.
  • Presenter owns orchestration — it listens for grid edits, mutates the in-memory bean, calls the domain formula, and pushes the new total to the view. It calls formulas; it never contains them.
  • Service owns load and commit — it fetches the whole object graph in one path and flushes it transactionally, mirroring a Forms COMMIT.
  • Data is Spring's JdbcClient (chosen over jOOQ to sidestep Oracle-dialect licensing).

The three headline constructs

Forms constructVaadin targetThe honest seam
Execute / Enter Query (F7/F8) A persistent filter bar + a lazy, paged data provider over S_ORD We replace the modal query mode rather than replicate it. We give up arbitrary QBE expressiveness for a curated filter set — but it demonstrably pages against the DB, never loads the whole table.
Product LOV A type-ahead lookup backed by the LOV's record-group query Near-direct analogue of the LOV idiom.
Master-detail block Master = single-select Grid with deselect disabled; detail = inline-editable line-items grid Grid commits per cell; Forms validates per item on navigation. A documentable difference, not a bug.

Transaction and locking: "we did not touch your database"

We commit the master + detail graph as one transaction, and we do optimistic locking with ORA_ROWSCN — read on load, re-check in UPDATE … WHERE id = ? AND ORA_ROWSCN = ?; zero rows updated means a conflict, so roll back. No schema change. That is the credibility claim a DBA will test first, and it holds. We document the ROWDEPENDENCIES block-vs-row SCN-precision caveat as an honest finding rather than hiding it.

Some things you don't migrate — and they keep working

The boundary rule: table-level / data-integrity logic stays in the database; form-serving logic moves to the Java service layer; logic the new architecture absorbs simply dissolves.

  • The AUDIT_S_ITEM trigger (AFTER INSERT) stays in the DB, untouched. It fires transparently inside the Vaadin commit's transaction — zero Java written. The one bridge: we set Oracle's CLIENT_IDENTIFIER per request from the Spring Security principal (~5 lines), so the trigger keeps recording the real human despite a pooled service account.
  • The get_product_image function dissolves into the product lookup query — the data provider already fetches the row, so the filename just comes along.

Styling is dropped; structure is not

This is the subtlest line we drew, and we got it wrong once before getting it right — which is exactly the kind of thing this POC exists to surface.

We made the Aura theme the single owner of visual styling. Forms' per-field fonts, colours, bevels and visual-attribute groups are dropped, not translated. Migrated screens are not pixel-identical to Forms, on purpose.

The mistake we caught

Our first pass over-reached: it dropped field geometry wholesale — and geometry encodes structure, not just pixels. The migrated ORDERS header came out with its fields reordered, its bordered "Order Information" group gone, its section title missing, and its PAYMENT_TYPE radio flattened to a text field. The spec census still cheerfully read "183 elements, nothing dropped."

That gap — counted ≠ rendered — produced two corrections, both now first-class rules:

  • Structural layout fidelity is migrated. Field order, frame grouping, and section titles are preserved (derived from geometry, then geometry itself is dropped). A view is not "done" until a layout-fidelity test asserts every in-scope item, frame and heading renders, in the form's order, as its mapped component type.
  • Read-only is a state, not a component type. A read-only slice still renders the control the classifier mapped — a disabled RadioButtonGroup, not a TextField printing CASH. The component type comes from the ruleset; read-only is just a runtime state on top.

The lesson generalizes well past this form: a behaviour-only test passes even when the screen is wrong. Layout fidelity needs its own gate.

The method: three skills, one validation loop

The reason corrections can be routed to the right place is that the tooling is three separate boxes, not one black box.

  • 1 · forms-xml-analyzer — turns frmf2xml output into a faithful, decision-free structural spec: every block, item, trigger, relation, LOV, frame and label, recorded verbatim. No Vaadin knowledge, no migration decisions. Its completeness guarantee is at form-object grain — every node accounted for, testable against the XSD. (For ORDERS: 183 elements, 4 blocks, 34 items, 45 triggers, 1 LOV.)
  • 2 · The mapping ruleset (migration-rules.yaml) — the published IP. A first-match-wins decision tree that maps each Forms construct to a Vaadin target: a numeric text item → NumberField; an LOV-bound item → ComboBox; Radio Group → RadioButtonGroup; a Forms frame → grouping section; a table audit trigger → stays in DB. It is property-aware and carries an explicit "Aura ignore list" so visual attributes have one disposition, not dozens of bespoke ones. This file is the living substrate of the generalizable-vs-specific sort.
  • 3 · Generic spec-driven-dev skills — consume spec + ruleset, cluster form objects into construct-grain tickets (~7, one per thing an architect recognizes), publish them as GitHub issues, and generate code. The clustering step is the architectural-decision step.

The build loop

Per construct — riskiest first — not per whole-POC:

  • Generate the construct from its ticket.
  • Validate against the live Forms app (the behavioural oracle) and diagnose which layer failed: bad ticket → fix the ruleset; ticket right but code buggy → fix the execution skill; irreducible form quirk → hand-fix, touch no skill.
  • Sort every fix — generalizable into the ruleset (regenerate; now works for every form) or specific (stays manual, logged).
  • Stop when it compiles and matches the live form on the spine flow. Cap refinement at ~2 passes per construct. If a construct won't converge — stop and write it up. Non-convergence is the most valuable finding, not a reason to grind.

When a Forms pattern has no obvious web shape: prototype it

Most constructs have a defensible target in the ruleset. Some don't — and the riskiest mistake is to let the first idea harden into code.

The clearest example was the master block itself. Forms' S_ORD block is single-record Execute/Enter-Query: you query, you land on one order, and a record scrollbar walks you through the result set. The web has no native idiom for that. There are at least three plausible renderings, and they imply very different apps — picking wrong shapes navigation app-wide.

So before writing a line of Vaadin, we built a throwaway prototype: one static HTML page, three radically different UI variants toggleable from a single switcher, all running off the same mock order data. Cheap to build, cheap to throw away, and — crucially — something you can put side by side against the live Forms app.

VariantShapeVerdict
A — lookup search → one order + prev/next Quick search + advanced filter panel; one match loads a header FormLayout + line-items grid; prev/next walks the result set. Chosen It's what the block-master-single rule already encodes, and it keeps single-record fidelity — QBE becomes a curated filter, the record scrollbar becomes a prev/next seam.
B — results grid → inline detail Search returns a grid of orders; clicking a row loads its detail underneath. Rejected More "webby", but it resurrects a master grid the ruleset explicitly rejects and breaks single-record fidelity.
C — search list → routed detail page A results list you navigate from; the order opens on its own focused route. Rejected The most conventional web CRUD shape — a good fit for a different app, but too far from the Forms original for a migration claiming fidelity.

The prototype's job is to make the decision visible and reversible — you compare three real screens instead of arguing about three descriptions. Once Variant A won, the verdict was recorded (with explicit reasons for the rejections), the winning shape was folded into the real OrderView, and the two losing variants were deleted. The prototype survives as a read-only mock of the chosen shape — the prototype code was never promoted as-is.

Two rules keep this phase honest

Prototype the pattern, not the product. It's a sketch to settle one question — here, "what is the faithful web rendering of single-record Execute/Enter-Query?" — built in throwaway HTML, not the real stack. It is allowed to be ugly and fake its data.

The decision flows back into the ruleset. Variant A won because it matched an existing rule, and that rule's guidance was then enriched with the quick+advanced search affordance the prototype validated. A prototype that discovers a genuinely new pattern earns a new rule (and, if it overturns one, an ADR). The prototype is where an unmapped pattern becomes a mapped one.

What we actually built, construct by construct

Each of these shipped behind a real browser test (Playwright) running against a real Oracle (Testcontainers), exercised end-to-end through all five layers:

  • #10Quick search → read-only header. The tracer bullet: type an order id, load one order through the whole stack.
  • #11Read-only line-items grid. S_ORD_S_ITEM coordination; header and lines load and reload together.
  • #12App shell + layout topology. Canvas / toolbar / CONTROL block folded into a Vaadin app shell.
  • #13Prev/next pager. "Record N of M" over the result set.
  • #14Advanced search panel. A curated filter bar with Clear, replacing Enter-Query; navigation reflects the active search.
  • #15Order total. The Sum summary as a pure domain method plus a live grid footer.
  • #16Inline line-item editing. In progress — editable quantities, add/delete lines, per-order id assignment, live total recompute, and a cascade-delete guard.

The remaining spine — product swap via the LOV (re-defaulting price and description) and the ORA_ROWSCN commit path — is next.

Reproducibility: a guaranteed tier and an honest tier

  • Tier 1 — guaranteed. Clone, docker compose up, run. The Summit slice runs against a self-contained Oracle Free container seeded from a committed dump (75 tables, ~54k rows; the POC slice — S_ORD 3,725 rows, S_ITEM 12,509 — loads intact). A stranger needs Docker, not an Oracle licence or your Forms DB.
  • Tier 2 — honest. The skills + the mapping ruleset + the actual prompt transcript that produced this. Applied to your form, the method gives you a classified migration backlog — recommended target per construct, decisions flagged, nothing dropped — not a finished app.

The single most trust-building sentence we can write: this reproduces the Summit migration exactly; on your own form it gives you a documented head start, not a finished product — and here's precisely where you'll still work.

What this means for a Forms shop

If you are sitting on a few hundred Oracle Forms, the takeaway is not "AI will rewrite them for you." It is sharper and more useful than that:

  • AI does a large fraction of each construct unaided, and that fraction is measurable.
  • The corrections it needs sort cleanly into teach the tool once vs fix this one form by hand — and the first bucket compounds across your whole form estate.
  • The genuinely hard parts (arbitrary QBE, modal validation semantics, pixel-fidelity) are knowable in advance and small in number. You can plan around them instead of discovering them mid-project.

The ratio is the number. This POC is how you measure it on one form before you bet a migration program on it.

Built with Vaadin 25, Spring Boot 4, Oracle Free, and a set of composable AI migration skills. The ruleset, the ADRs behind every decision above, and the full spec for the ORDERS form are in this repository.
